titleStmt.title: Impact of entrepreneurial leadership on project success: mediating role of knowledge management processes

analytic.title: Impact of entrepreneurial leadership on project success: mediating role of knowledge management processes

biblStruct.note: Received 15 July 2019 Revised 28 October 2019 6 January 2020 Accepted 10 January 2020

div.p: Purpose -Drawing on the knowledge-based view (KBV), the study investigates the impact of entrepreneurial leadership (EL) on knowledge management (KM) processes and further examines the mediating role of KM processes on the linkage between EL and project success (PS). Design/methodology/approach -Survey data were collected from 304 project workers in software projects, and the proposed relationships were assessed through SMART-PLS structural equation modeling tool. Findings -The study found a significant impact of EL on KM processes and PS. The analysis also revealed that KM processes significantly impact project success while EL impact PS indirectly through KM processes. Originality/value -The relevancy of the research stems from the scarcity of research on EL, while studies on the role of leadership as a predictor of KM are significantly limited. Additionally, there is a scarcity of research on the impact of KM on project success. This is one of the earliest studies that investigate the inter-relationship among EL, KM processes and project success.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Business practices around the world have raised some difficult issues for managers with respect to leadership styles. Leaders should concentrate on taking initiatives, risk-taking and building competitiveness in order to achieve goals and guarantee a sustained competitive advantage (Gil et al., 2018;Villaluz and Hechanova, 2019). The knowledge-based view (KBV) (Grant, 1996) recognizes knowledge as a critical asset which, if managed effectively, can lead an organization towards the achievement of competitive advantage and better project performance. Leaders are the core assets to manage knowledge effectively (Bryant, 2003).

Leaders have an uninterrupted impact on how the organizations should approach and manage KM processes (Singh, 2008). KBV assumes that KM processes such as knowledge acquisition, creation, storage, sharing/transform and knowledge application/utilization play a critical role in achieving better performance and competitive advantage (Shujahat et al., 2019). 21st-century organizations keep on confronting changes particularly with the improvement and speeding up of innovation, ordinary leadership may not be an alternative and EL is the response to survival and accomplishment for present-day organizations (Abubakar et al., 2018).

EL is an emerging paradigm and is the blend of business entrepreneurship and leadership which at whatever point associated will enable the organization to exploit the opportunity to attain the upper hand (Huang et al., 2014;Abubakar et al., 2018). EL as the leadership style and behavior can encourage development and performance in unverifiable, challenging and aggressive conditions (Al Mamun et al., 2018;Strobl et al., 2018). The need for entrepreneurial leaders in businesses is increasing and the subject of EL requires further attention of researchers (Al Mamun et al., 2018).

The need to study entrepreneurial leadership stems from the fact that scholars have shown concern towards the effectiveness of general leadership styles (e.g. transformational/ transactional) in directing employees' involvement in the challenging tasks of project management for two main reasons. First, general leadership styles are not specifically designed to regulate employees' behavior and second, they do not determine the leader's exact behavior and techniques to direct different complex project-related processes (Andersen et al., 2006). Leaders of high technology businesses, defined as the businesses that allocate significantly high financial resources to scientific, technological, research and development activities (Butchart, 1987), need to develop new leadership competencies in order to effectively manage the processes in their business (Chen et al., 2014). An increasing number of studies have highlighted entrepreneurial leadership as the leadership style and behavior that significantly stimulates and fosters innovation and opportunity recognition in highly challenging, turbulent and competitive environments (Freeman and Siegfried, 2015). Yet, there is a considerable lack of research on the effects of this leadership style in projectbased organizations and the success of the projects.

Organizational leadership has been identified as a prominent KM enabler (Iqbal et al., 2019;Obeidat et al., 2016). The emerging EL style has gained particular interest in performance management research in project-based organizations due to their relevance to the project-based organizations and their management (Abubakar et al., 2018;Mishra and Misra, 2017;Zainol et al., 2018). Scholars have described and assessed KM enablers and KM processes as KM capability (Iqbal et al., 2019;Al-Hakim and Hassan, 2011). KM processes include practices pertinent to knowledge acquisition, creation, sharing and utilization that foster sustainable competitive advantage (Torres et al., 2018). Existing literature has identified a number of gaps in relation to the role of EL, KM processes and project success that shall be addressed.

First, although the interest in EL has been growing, the concept of EL is still significantly under-developed (Dean and Ford, 2017;Harrison et al., 2018;Strobl et al., 2018). The various parts of leadership literature have yet to permeate the field of entrepreneurship (Leitch and Volery, 2017).

Second, researchers have recently begun to investigate the role of leaders in KM (Mato skov a et al., 2018;Naqshbandi and Jasimuddin, 2018;Donate and de Pablo, 2015). Existing research has assessed the impact of leadership on a limited number of KM processes (Bavik et al., 2018). Masa'deh et al. (2017) stressed that the KM processes, in particular, knowledge sharing, has been well researched. Hence, the present study has taken into consideration four KM processes: Knowledge Acquisition, Knowledge Storage, Knowledge Sharing, and Knowledge Utilization.

Third, the relationship between leadership and organizational performance is studied in light of different mediating variables (Fu et al., 2018;Kantur, 2016;Al-Dhaafri et al., 2016). The direct relationship between EL and project success can be questionable. Existing research has called for an assessment of KM processes as a mediating variable that could explain the impact of leadership on different organizational level outcomes (Chang et al., 2018;Nasab and Afshari, 2019;Naqshbandi and Jasimuddin, 2018).

Fourth, the impact of KM has been investigated on project-based outcomes (Project Performance and Success). Existing research has evaluated the impact of a limited number of KM processes on project success (see Yang et al., 2012;Fedor et al., 2003). Showing that research on knowledge management in project management literature is still in its infancy (Bavik et al., 2018).

This research intends to fill the identified knowledge gaps and in doing so makes several contributions. First, the study extends the limited research on the understanding of EL (Cai, 2018) and its impact on project success. Our study is among the first to consider EL as an important antecedent of project success. Second, the study investigates whether EL can serve as an important predictor of KM processes as the role of leadership as a predictor of KM processes is significantly limited (Bavik et al., 2018;Shamim et al., 2019). Third, the study further assesses whether KM processes mediate the relationship between EL and project success. This would help in providing a basis for understanding the mediating mechanism through which EL affects knowledge management processes and ultimately result in a successful project. Understanding the mechanisms that lead to the effect of EL on project success would help to articulate a better theoretical understanding of this relationship. Fourth, there is significantly limited research on how different KM processes impact project success. The research would enrich the knowledge management literature and help understand the role of KM in fostering improved project success. The research contributes to the leadership literature by assessing a new form of leadership style and its implication towards knowledge management and project success. Additionally, the study would provide further insights to KBV by demonstrating how EL contributes towards KM processes that lead to a successful project. Through the integration of KBV, we identify the KM process as a distinct pathway through which EL is associated with project success.

div.head: Literature review
div.p: Entrepreneurial leadership (EL) Cunningham and Lischeron (1991) began the research on EL who suggested that it refers to setting clear goals, creating chances, allowing people, safeguarding organizational understanding and creating human resource frameworks. Recently, Renko et al. (2015) stressed that EL involves inducing and directing the performance of group members towards the attainment of organizational goals through recognition and exploitation of entrepreneurial opportunities. Chen (2007) depicts that EL helps to enhance the success of the leader's task achievement and efficiency. Conceptualized by McGrath and Macmillan (2000) who stressed that the competitive pressures and increasing uncertainty in the globalized dynamic market require a new type of leader. Thus, they gave the description of the "entrepreneurial leader" as the one who has an apt "entrepreneurial" approach and precisely the ability to keep abreast with the fast-changing markets, and to exploit opportunities to gather advantages before and faster than others (Karmarkar et al., 2014). Entrepreneurial leadership is a unique leadership style that is focused on making heterogeneous talents work more creatively and innovatively in collective processes to respond to the uncertain business environment to create a coherent strategy and novel outcomes. Hence, organizations need to be able to measure and thus manage their entrepreneurial leadership (Musa and Fontana, 2016).

Entrepreneurs operating enterprises function as the leader of their business and need specific leadership skills to launch, grow, and sustain a successful venture. In the increasingly turbulent and competitive environment business firms face today, a type of "entrepreneurial" leader distinct from other behavioral forms of leadership is required (Gupta et al., 2004). Transformational leaders demonstrate some features and behaviors that also characterize entrepreneurial leaders; hence, there may be an overlap (Gupta et al., 2004). For instance, intellectual stimulation could be an overlap between the two leadership styles. Leaders seek new ways of working, seek opportunities in face of risk and are not likely to support the status quo. Instead of adapting to environmental circumstances, transformational leaders attempt to create and shape them (Lowe et al., 1996). Finnie and Early (2002) noted that entrepreneurial leaders go beyond the traditional concept of being a charismatic or transformational leader. The need to address the fast-paced and ever-changing business environment gave birth to the concept of entrepreneurial leadership. This ever-evolving dynamic business environment has required leaders to be transformative, as well as innovative and proactive while managing risk (Tarabishy et al., 2005). If a business is facing turbulence, attributed to new venture development, industry changes, or organizational change, entrepreneurial leadership style could lead to the willingness of the leader to take risks and contribute innovative ideas to lead the organization to a point of stability (Cai, 2018). In transformational leadership, the leader arouses follower performance by enticing to the higher follower needs. However, the entrepreneurial leader's ability to evoke such performance is founded in the context of the firm's need to adapt to emerging environmental contingencies. Thus, the basic challenge is to create a willingness in followers to abandon conventional but career-secure activities for creative, entrepreneurial action (Gupta et al., 2004).

It is apparent that entrepreneurial and transformational leadership styles are different (Renko et al., 2015). Transformational leadership is based on inspiring followers to attain organizational goals but also accomplish personal goals. Though individualized consideration is critical to the transformational leadership style, it is not an ingredient of entrepreneurial leadership. Individualized consideration provides support to followers to help them reach self-actualization (Northouse, 2016). Transformational leaders recognize the unique needs and abilities of their employees, treat employees as individuals, build one-to-one relationships and comprehend and are considerate about their differing skills (Avolio and Bass, 1995). Entrepreneurial leaders, consider employees in terms of their entrepreneurial passion and self-efficacy. They enhance followers' beliefs in their own entrepreneurial skills and abilities and ignite the passion for innovation and creativity (Cai, 2018). The center to the entrepreneurial leadership is the emphasis on opportunity-oriented behaviors, by both leaders and those who follow them. Though transformational leadership has some characteristics of such behaviors, they are not endemic.

Leaders with entrepreneurial characteristics may lack inspiration or charisma that is typically characteristic of transformational leaders (Renko et al., 2015). Entrepreneurial leaders also motivate and inspire subordinates through imitation by role modeling instead of inspiring others to personal achievements. Although they lead with clear purpose and goals, entrepreneurial leaders may not be described as charismatic or inspirational by others as often as transformational leaders (Podsakoff et al., 1990). Although a transformational leader uses charisma, inspirational appeals, dramatic presentations, symbolism, or other forms of impression management to inspire admiration, respect, and loyalty, and entrepreneurial leadercharismatic or notacts as a role model in entrepreneurial behavior, inspiring imitation. In comparing transactional leadership style to the entrepreneurial leadership style, entrepreneurial leadership is more transformational than transactional (Yang, 2008). Some scholars have posited that transformational and transactional leadership styles often depict the leader as someone entrusted with an organizational task that needs to be accomplished within a given organizational context (Gupta et al., 2004). On the contrary, entrepreneurial leadership is founded on the assumption that the leader must enact an entirely emergent organizational task, not one that is carefully planned, and uncover an entirely emergent transaction set, not originally visualized (Gupta et al., 2004;Wang et al., 2012). Thus, under the challenge of high ambiguity and uncertainty, it may have an increasing demand for entrepreneurial leadership (Chen, 2007). These distinct behaviors of the entrepreneurial leadership style making it a distinguished style of leadership whose implications shall be further elaborated.

div.head: LODJ 41,2
div.p: Knowledge management processes (KMPR) According to Jain (2007) KM processes are operationally characterized as intentional management procedure to catch, create, store, transform, share and apply both understood and express information to serve workers, organizations and its clients. According to Obeidat et al. (2016) in the manifold, rapidly changing and uncertain situation, management of knowledge turns out to be one of the most important and interesting concepts in management. Knowledge management has four main processes including knowledge acquisition, knowledge storage, knowledge sharing and knowledge utilization (Sadeghi and Rad, 2018;Costa and Monteiro, 2016). Knowledge Acquisition (KA) refers to the proactive initiatives implemented by the project to identify and collect relevant information from external sources that are critical to its operations (Ali et al., 2018). Knowledge Storage (KST) refers to storing, combining, organizing, structuring, getting and connecting advance capacity, for example, reports, phone directories and pictures with knowledge units (Lin, 2013). Knowledge Sharing (KSH) refers to acts of making knowledge available to others within the organization (Ipe, 2003, p. 32). Knowledge Utilization (KU) is the application of information for the attainment of business goals (Asoh et al., 2007).

div.head: Project success (PS)
div.p: Project success has been a central topic in project management literature and project success criteria are measures used to evaluate the success or failure of a project (Al-Tmeemy et al., 2011). Operationally, project is defined as a unique and temporary effort that must be completed within a specified budget, time and scope. Jugdev et al. (2013) divide project success into two segments, whereby project success elements (critical factors) are related to independent variables that contribute to the project towards the achievement and second segment is project success standards; these are measures used to assess if a project was successful or failure. Shenhar et al. (2002) claimed that project success could be influenced by various factors in different types of projects and for that, an organization shall make adjustments in order to deal with the effect of different factors that could affect the chances of project success or failure.

div.head: Entrepreneurial leadership and project success
div.p: In project-based organizations, effective leadership improves the commitment by instilling a positive attitude and culture that aids in the achievement of project success (Aga et al., 2016). According to Nixon et al. (2012), leadership is one of the viable tools utilized by project managers to impact the project result. Under the pressure of competitive situations different project-based organizations, utilize project leaders to react quickly to the environmental changes and achieve the organizational objectives. Existing literature on leadership identifies different leadership styles and their positive effect on project success and management of the organization (Aga et al., 2016;Raziq et al., 2018).

Leaders can benefit from entrepreneurial competencies to deal with the highly turbulent and competitive environment of modern organizations (Luu, 2017). Success through entrepreneurship can be achieved when employees are encouraged and nurtured (Shepherd et al., 2009). Entrepreneurial effort refers to key challenges managers face and is related to the "extent to which top managers are inclined to take business-related risks (the risk-taking dimension), to favor change and innovation to obtain a competitive advantage for their firm (the innovation dimension) and to compete aggressively with other firms (the proactiveness dimension)" (Covin and Slevin, 1988, p. 218).

The relationship between the EL and PS is not clear and has not to be assessed yet, however, literature shows that organizations with a higher level of entrepreneurial characteristics tend to perform better (Rauch et al., 2009). Thus, understanding project success is as important as understanding EL, and the aspects of both concepts are presented in this section. Project-oriented companies have their results closely related to the success of the projects they develop. In this sense, the evidence from the literature that EL contributes to different performance-related outcomes, for instance, EL style is positively linked with organizational level performance (Abubakar et al., 2018;Al Mamun et al., 2018;Huang et al., 2014;Zainol et al., 2018), the performance of group members towards achieving organizational goals (Renko et al., 2015) and merger and acquisition performance (Strobl et al., 2018). Additionally, like other leadership styles (transformational and transactional leadership styles) that have shown their significant impact on project success (Zaman et al., 2019;Aga, 2016), it can be assumed that EL will have a significant impact on project success. Entrepreneurship has been identified as a well-known path to the achievement of growth and strategic renewal (Hitt et al., 2002). This offers the possibility of a relationship between EL and project success.

In a study developed with leaders and employees, Ahmed et al. (2014) showed that entrepreneurial individuals on project teams increase a project's success. Studies also relate project management to innovation (Gordon and Tarafdar, 2007), to the ideas for improvement and development of products, processes, and services (Meredith and Mantel, 2003), to risktaking (Vezzoni et al., 2013), creativity in solving problems (Al-Tmeemy et al., 2011), to proactiveness (Kerzner, 2004) and change (McLeod et al., 2012) in current ways of doing business. An entrepreneurial leader can provide the team members with an open environment that supports collaboration, knowledge sharing and one where team members can come up with solutions to the problems (Renko et al., 2015) and this can aid during the course of the project and make it more successful (Sohmen, 2013). The aforementioned factors are key characteristics of EL and have been found to have an effect in project-based organizations. Thus, considering the context just presented, the following hypothesis is proposed:
H1. There is a significant impact of entrepreneurial leadership on project success.

div.head: Mediating role of knowledge management
div.p: Effective leadership can act as a critical instrument in sharing information and knowledge within the organization, so timely and realistic decisions can be taken (Chang et al., 2019). Wei et al. (2009) referred to leadership as a KM enabler that enables an organization to align KM behaviors with opportunities, organizational strategies, communicate the best strategies, facilitate the evolution of learning organizations, promote the values of KM, and provide metrics for ascertaining the impact of knowledge. Hence, leadership incorporates strategic issues and how an organization defines its business and uses its knowledge resources to strengthen its competencies (Jager, 1999). Without the commitment of leadership, it is difficult to achieve the success of KM (Civi, 2000). Leaders assume a focal job during the way towards managing organization knowledge. Leaders give vision, motivation, systems and structures at all levels of the organization that improves learning (Bryant, 2003). There are some studies that show the role of leadership in knowledge management processes. For example, Bavik et al. (2018) investigated the relationship between ethical leadership and knowledge sharing and found leadership as a key factor influencing the process of knowledge sharing. Singh (2008) assessed the impact of different leadership styles (directive style of leadership, supportive style of leadership, consulting style of leadership and delegating style of leadership) on knowledge management practices in a software firm of India.

KBV recognizes knowledge as the most strategically important of the firm' s resources while EL is committed to the discovery and exploitation of strategic value creation (Gupta et al., 2004). EL is about taking the risk (Kuratko, 2007) while from a knowledge management perspective, an organization's system that fosters experimentation and risk-taking aids learning, knowledge creation and dissemination (Mikkelsen et al., 2000). Wong and Aspinall (2004) proposed that successful knowledge management requires proactive EL. Their study demonstrated that leadership must create an organizational culture in which there is employee cooperation and knowledge sharing. According to KBV, knowledge is created, stored, and utilized by individuals and not by organizations as a whole, coordinating and integrating the knowledge held by individuals is a difficult task (Miles, 2012). This can be made possible through EL which is characterized by their ability as an integrator and informed (Huang et al., 2014).

KBV identifies knowledge as a key resource and a strategic asset that empowers the business to create value (Zack et al., 2009). In light of KBV (Grant, 1996), successful utilization of knowledge-based resources and effective implementation of KM processes is imperative to achieve better performance (Mazdeh and Hesamamiri, 2014). KBV supports the idea that when knowledge is effectively managed, it creates distinguishing capabilities that contribute to improved performance (Leal-Rodr ıguez et al., 2013). There is an increasing need for the use of knowledge management as an enabler to improve organization outcomes (Hsiao et al., 2011). With the organizations facing rapid changes both within and outside the organization, knowledge-related capabilities can provide significant support in sustaining competitive advantage and be successful (Torres et al., 2018;Shahzad et al., 2016). For example, KM processes such as acquisition, sharing and utilization not only support learning and decisionmaking but also drive productivity and profitability through innovative ideas and novelty (Chiu and Chen, 2016).

Entrepreneurial leadership involves a creative and proactive response to environmental opportunities (Brown and Duguid, 1991). From this perspective, entrepreneurial leaders are experts who have learned which problems are relevant to their domain and how to solve them and create a knowledge-based environment that that facilitates problem-solving and value creation (Surie and Ashley, 2008). In a constantly changing external environment, organizational members feel high ambiguity and exert pressure on leaders to respond with new knowledge, skills, and processes (Jansen et al., 2009). From a human capital perspective, entrepreneurial leaders focus on improving an individual's knowledge, skills and capabilities (Leitch et al., 2013); they respond and innovate by broadening existing knowledge and skills (Huang et al., 2014). According to Chen (2007), the entrepreneurial team looks to an entrepreneurial leader for vision, guidance, selection of team members for different assignments, and creating the necessary environment to facilitate innovation, encourage creativity, and facilitate knowledge creation and knowledge sharing. In their role as accelerators, entrepreneurial leaders also make followers rethink their jobs from the perspective of entrepreneurial opportunities that can be recognized through their specific knowledge and skill areas.

Knowledge management processes are rapidly becoming an integral business activity for organizations and it consists of a dynamic and continuous set of processes and practices directed to identifying and leveraging the collective knowledge in an organization to help the organization compete (Garrido-Moreno et al., 2015). Knowledge management plays a significant role in enhancing projects that are used to improve an organization's performance and to sustain a competitive advantage in the market (Jaleel et al., 2019). Therefore, in today's changing environment, management of knowledge is necessary for project success (Polyaninova, 2011). Knowledge management is turning into an imperative vital issue in project management (Yang et al., 2012). KM is critical for project success due to its critical role in knowledge sharing and communication (Solomon, 2001). Through KM, firms look to gain or make conceivably helpful knowledge and to make it accessible to the individuals to impact organizational performance (King, 2009). As per Love et al. (2003) poor use of KM adversely influences project success. KM has been displayed as a practice that helps to improve projects, in this way, KM is seen as the best approach to improve efficiency and increment benefit if knowledge resources are utilized adequately (Alghaila et al., 2017). If organizations desire to maintain good standing in the industry and hold a competitive advantage by a high number of successful project implementations, they should not only rely on the traditional project management improvement techniques but also act to manage their knowledge-of-projects. Moreover, organizations need to employ an efficient KM strategy towards the successful completion of projects. Such a strategy may focus on processes to capture, organize and share the knowledge (Jaleel et al., 2019). KM is important in relation to projects because knowledge related processes affect project performance in terms of costs, schedule, and quality (Berteaux and Javernick-Will, 2015). KM processes (For instance, knowledge sharing and KM utilization) are significant in avoiding the repetition of past mistakes at both the project and organizational levels and improve the chance of project success (Javernick-Will and Hartmann, 2011;Waters and Beruvides, 2012). In addition, organizations face challenges in improving project performance and addressing the risks of project failure, further highlighting the significance of the role of knowledge management and its impact on project success (Anantatmula, 2010). Several studies have identified knowledge management to improve organizational performance (Iqbal et al., 2019;Shahzad et al., 2016). Very few published empirical studies have focused on the direct effect of knowledge management on project performance. While Yang et al. (2012) and Yang et al. (2017) found a significant impact of KM on project success, the relationship was moderately significant in the study of Fedor et al. (2003). Managers in project-based organizations, regardless of their work environment or industry, agree on how important proper knowledge asset management is to project success (Lierni and Ribi ere, 2008). Researchers have indicated ways in which project knowledge can be protected and utilized to enable individuals to make good decisions using actionable information, experience, and insight (Lierni and Ribi ere, 2008). Hence, there is a lack of conclusive evidence on the linkage between the two concepts.

Leadership commitment to effective knowledge management in the context of a projectbased business strategy is emerging as a potent means of establishing and sustaining competitive advantage (Ajmal et al., 2010) ultimately leading to continued project success. The literature leads to the belief that EL connects with improved KM processes that enhance the chances of project success (see Figure 1). Accordingly, the study argues that KM processes play a mediating role in the relationship between EL and project success. Based on the literature it is proposed that H2. There is a significant impact of entrepreneurial leadership on KM Processes.
H3. There is a significant impact of KM processes on project success.

H4. KM processes mediate the relationship between entrepreneurial leadership and project success. Research methodology Software technology firms make up the sample for the study since these companies probably have a broader spectrum of KM strategies (Donate and Pablo, 2015), In addition, knowledge organizations from technology-intensive industries require a different management approach from non-knowledge organizations, and the role of leadership should be distinctive and supportive of KM processes (Yahya and Goh, 2002). A total of 304 sample size was achieved. The demographic profile of respondents for this study showed that they are typically males, The average age of the respondents was 26.836 years. The majority of the respondents holds a bachelor's degree, work as an android developer and have experienced between 1-10 years. The questionnaire used a seven-point Likert scale from "1" referring to "strongly disagree" to "7" referring to "strongly agree". EL construct compromises eight items ENTRELEAD scale and is adapted from (Renko et al., 2015), example items include My manager demonstrates passion for my work and My manager has a vision of the future of our business. Knowledge management processes were measured using processes: knowledge acquisition, knowledge storage, knowledge sharing, and knowledge utilization. These dimensions of KMP are measured using 33 adopted items. Knowledge acquisition, knowledge sharing, and knowledge utilization scale were adapted from (Gold et al., 2001). Knowledge acquisition has a total of eight items, sample items include Our organization has processes for generating new knowledge from existing knowledge and Our organization uses feedback from projects to improve subsequent projects. Knowledge sharing has a total of ten items, example items include Our organization has processes for transferring organizational knowledge to individuals and Our organization has processes for distributing knowledge throughout the organization. Knowledge utilization has a total of seven items, example items include Our organization has processes for applying the knowledge learned from errors and Our organization has processes for using knowledge to solve new problems. Knowledge storage is measured using eight items adopted from the study of (Donate and Guadamillas, 2010), example items include In our organization the organizational procedures are documented through work procedures, written protocols, handbooks, etc. and In our organization IT is used to handle, structure, and improve the quality of information and knowledge and encourage communication and accessibility among individuals. The project success constructs compromises of six items based on the work on Aga et al. (2016), example items include The project was completed on time and the project was completed according to the budget allocated. Data analysis was performed using SmartPLS 3.2.8.

div.head: Measurement model
div.p: The measurement model displays the relationships between the constructs and the indicator variables. As part of the measurement model evaluation, indicators with low factor loadings (< 0.60) were removed (Gefen and Straub, 2005). Only one item (KA1) was removed from the analysis due to low factor loading. The first component of the measurement model is the reliability analysis which includes composite reliability. The desirable cutoff value for the composite reliability is 0.70 (Ringle et al., 2018). Consequently, all the latent constructs of the model possess composite reliability (Table 1). The second component of the measurement model is convergent validity. The measure of convergent validity is the Average Variance Extracted (AVE) for which the cut-off criterion value is 0.50 (Ringle et al., 2018). Hence, constructs possess convergent validity (see Table 1). The component used to access the discriminant validity of the constructs is the Heterotrait Monotrait (HTMT) Ratio procedure. As indicated by Henseler et al. (2015), to check for the discriminant validity, the most conservative threshold values of HTMT ratio is less than or

div.head: Structural model
div.p: The structural model displays the relationships (paths) between the constructs on the proposed study model. H1 evaluates whether EL is positively related to PS. The results revealed that EL has a significant impact (total effect) on PS (β 5 0.645, t 5 13.836, p < 0.0001). Hence, H1 was supported. H2 evaluates whether EL has a significant impact on KM. The results show that EL has a significant impact on KM (β 5 0.777, t 5 22.554, p < 0.001). Consequently, H2 was supported. H3 evaluates whether KM is positively related to PS. The results revealed that KM has a significant impact on PS (β 5 0.624, t 5 8.343, p < 0.001). Consequently, H3 is accepted. The results are presented in Table 3.

div.head: Mediation analysis
div.p: Lastly, H4 evaluates whether KM mediates the relationship between EL and PS. The results show that the total effect (H1) was found positive and significant (β 5 0.645, t 5 13.836, p < 0.001). When the mediator was introduced into the model the effect was decreased and the direct relationship was found insignificant (β 5 0.160, t 5 1.923, p > 0.05) while the indirect effect with the inclusion of mediator into the analysis was found significant (β 5 0.485, t 5 7.752, p < 0.001). Hence, the results reveal a complete mediation. This shows that the effect of EL on project success passes completely through KM. Consequently, H4 is accepted (see Table 4).

div.head: Discussion
div.p: The study is set out to establish the relationship between EL, KM processes, and PS. The acceptance of proposed relationships confirms the knowledge-based view. The study found a significant impact of EL on project success. The outcomes affirm this recommendation and

div.head: Entrepreneurial
div.p: leadership on project success are steady with the discoveries of the past examinations where the positive relationship between EL performance-based outcomes was found (Abubakar et al., 2018;Al Mamun et al., 2018;Renko et al., 2015;Strobl et al., 2018). This shows that a project-based organization characterized by leadership orientation towards risk, challenge, and passion will have a higher propensity for a successful project. This further strengthens the assertion that leaders can benefit from entrepreneurial competencies to deal with the highly turbulent and competitive environment (Gupta et al., 2004). Hence, an entrepreneurial leader can make provision for the team members where they have an open environment to come up with solutions to the problems, support collaboration, and knowledge sharing, (Renko et al., 2015) and this can aid during the course of the project and make it more successful (Sohmen, 2013).

The study found a significant impact of EL on KM processes. The results validated this hypothesis. Wong and Aspinall (2004) suggested that successful knowledge management requires proactive EL. Leadership conduct is an essential factor since leaders enormously affect the direction and effectiveness of KM inside their organizations (Donate and de Pablo, 2015;Singh, 2008). This shows that EL behaves like a dynamic capability, with a focus on the continuous reconfiguration of a firm's knowledge position through initiatives to articulate, codify, and utilize knowledge (Wang and Ahmed, 2007). A strong EL position forces the firm to embark on substantial investment and development initiatives pertinent to knowledge management (Donate and de Pablo, 2015).

The study found a significant impact of knowledge management processes on project success. Results validated this hypothesis and are consistent with the findings of the previous studies (Yang et al., 2012,Yang et al., 2017). The results demonstrate that the project-based organizations that utilize the knowledge management architecture can significantly improve the chances of making a successful project. This certified the validity of KBV that proposes that effective management of knowledge resources can facilitate organizations to achieve superior performance (Grant, 1996). This is achieved since, knowledge management can facilitate communications and provide more informed knowledge to the project manager and project team (Liebowitz and Megbolugbe, 2003).

Finally, the findings of this study provide important empirical insight into the indirect influence of EL on PS through the mediation of KM processes. The results show that KM processes mediate the relationship between EL and project success. The results are consistent with the findings of the previous studies which have found the significant mediating role of KM processes (Donate and de Pablo, 2015;Sadeghi and Rad, 2018;Sarkar et al., 2016). The chain of relationship holds true in light of KBV since the issues with which the KBV concerns itself include the organizational structure, the role of management (Grant, 1996).

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: The literature demonstrated a generally overlooked, but imperative constructs and ideas, EL and knowledge management processes that guarantee the success of a project. This paper presents one of the earliest attempts to develop and test an integrated model that links EL to project success through the mediating role of KM processes. This research adds to the leadership and KBV literature by exemplifying that EL can significantly enhance the KM processes that have a significant role in improving the chances of a successful project. The findings of this research render that EL is mandatory for successful implementation of KM processes and achieve project success. Policymakers and managers should come up with a deliberate plan to foster EL to encourage KM processes among their employees. Leadership or top management must promote entrepreneurial practices and must provide a clear vision about KM and share it with other members that KM processes are vital for the success of the project.

div.head: Implications
div.p: Theoretically, the substantiation of the proposed relationships sheds light on the contribution of EL and KM processes in leading to project success. More broadly, the article contributes to the development of studies linking entrepreneurship leadership, knowledge management, and project management, and strengthens the relationship evidenced in the literature that the EL contributes to organizational performance, in this study by contributing to the success of projects, hence, further highlighting the distinctiveness of EL in comparison to other leadership styles. Additionally, the article adds knowledge to studies seeking to understand the factors that influence the success in projects, as well as contributes to the list of benefits of EL for organizations. Taken into consideration the existing gap in the literature that addresses the relationship between EL and project success, this study aids in filling the gap in existing research and stimulate further research in the area. Furthermore, the study ascertains the role EL can play in fostering KM processes in project-based organizations that can use the KM processes to improve the chances of project success. The study explains the pathway through which EL can impact project success. Practically, comprehending the factors that could improve the chances of a successful project, directly and indirectly, could help organizations to get a competitive advantage. The validation of the proposed model points out to managers of the potency of developing EL skillset and improving KM processes in their respective organizations in the pursuit of project success. Thus, the findings suggest that practices of project management can be aligned to the firm's entrepreneurial leadership to enable firms to better result in their projects and generate competitive advantage. Given the proportion of the impact of EL on KM (57.1%) and EL and KM on project success (60.3%), it is important that project managers focus on improving their EL capabilities and improve KM processes within their organization that affect project success.

div.head: Research limitations and future research directions
div.p: The research study has a certain limitation that must be acknowledged. First, the data has been collected from the employees of the software industry of Pakistan; therefore, the model should be replicated in other contexts. Secondly, in the current study, only one leadership style has been tested, in future studies, other leadership styles should be tested such as authentic leadership, smart leadership, or charismatic leadership. Finally, in future studies with knowledge management processes, knowledge management approaches (social networking, codification, and personalization) should be tested as a mediator between different leadership styles and project success.
